source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Defines deliberate practice as activity designed to improve current performance. Conditions: well-defined task of suitable difficulty, informative feedback, repetition, error correction. Contrasts it with work and play. Claims performance level is tied to amount of deliberate practice and that practice is effortful and not inherently enjoyable.
numbers: Framework paper plus two studies. Work = paid performance, play = no goal, deliberate practice = designed to improve.
quote: the level of performance an individual attains is directly related to the amount of deliberate practice
limits: Definition is loose on who designs the activity (teacher vs self). Critics say this ambiguity let meta-analyses count very different activities.
agent_relevance: Background only. The agent does not practice, but the four conditions (goal, feedback, repetition, graded difficulty) map to a training loop, not to inference-time thinking.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Study 1 (Berlin violinists): three skill groups of 10 each (best, good, music-education) plus 10 middle-aged professionals. Groups matched on sex and age. Practice alone was rated most relevant to improvement by 27 of 30 violinists.
numbers: N=30 young violinists (10/10/10) plus 10 middle-aged professional violinists. Best group = 10 of 14 nominated as potential international soloists. Mean age about 23.
limits: Tiny groups, nominated by professors, so the group label is teacher judgment. Retrospective interview data. No blinding reported.
agent_relevance: Shows the paradigm later replications reuse: expert-vs-less-expert contrast on retrospective practice hours.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Core result of Study 1: accumulated solitary practice to age 18 ordered with skill. Best 7,410 h, good 5,301 h, music teachers 3,420 h. Middle-aged professionals 7,336 h, nearly equal to the best young group.
numbers: Best vs good F(1,27)=4.59, p<.05. Best+good vs teachers F(1,27)=11.86, p<.01. Mid-aged pros 7,336 h vs 7,410 h, n.s.
quote: there is complete correspondence between the skill level of the groups and their average accumulation of practice time alone
limits: Retrospective estimates; interviewer not blind to group (per the 2019 replication). Authors state complete correspondence between skill and practice.
agent_relevance: The 10,000 h figure comes from extrapolating this pattern to about age 20. It is a mean of one violin group, not a law.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Diary week in Study 1: the two top groups practised alone about 24.3 h per week versus 9.3 h for music teachers. About 3.5 h per day vs 1.3 h per day, every day including weekends. Sessions averaged 80 min with no group difference, so the difference was number of sessions (19.5 vs 7.1 per week).
numbers: Diary week, N=30. 24.3 vs 9.3 h, F(1,27)=44.05, p<.001. Sessions 19.5 vs 7.1 per week, F(1,27)=22.40. Total music-related time 50.6 h per week, no group difference.
limits: Single week of diary data. Typical-week estimates exceeded diary values by 5.2 h; 85% of top-group estimates were exact multiples of 7 (aspired level).
agent_relevance: Evidence that practice is capped by effort and fatigue. Sessions are limited to about 80 min.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Rest pattern in Study 1: top groups slept more (8.6 vs 7.8 h per day) and napped more (2.8 vs 0.9 h per week). Best violinists took less leisure (3.5 h per day vs 4.7 for good). Authors read this as recovery from effortful practice, with a daily cap of about 4 h.
numbers: Sleep 60.0 vs 54.6 h per week, F(1,27)=5.02, p<.05. Naps F(1,27)=5.92, p<.05. Leisure best vs good F(1,27)=4.27. Leisure vs music time r(28)=-0.37.
limits: Correlational. Rest could reflect general lifestyle, not a cause of skill.
agent_relevance: The 4 h per day ceiling is a claim about human effort limits. It has no counterpart for an LLM agent.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Study 2 (pianists): Berlin expert pianists vs matched amateurs. Experts had 7,606 h of accumulated practice by age 18 against 1,606 h for amateurs. Experts spent 56.75 h per week on music in the diary week vs 7.02 h.
numbers: Accumulated practice F(1,22)=26.29, p<.001. Diary 56.75 vs 7.02 h, F(1,22)=348. Leisure 4.66 h per day, no group difference. Practice overestimated by 5.2 h as in Study 1.
limits: Amateurs are a different population (mean start age 9.9). Experts vs amateurs is a much easier contrast than elite vs near-elite.
agent_relevance: Effect is far larger for a wide skill gap than for fine gaps among elites.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Study 2 performance tasks: accumulated practice predicted tapping and bimanual coordination about as well as skill-group membership did. Adding practice to skill group added a little within-group variance on complex tasks.
numbers: Table 2 R2 for skill level only: tapping right .55, left .43, alternate .47; single-hand .74, mirror .67, different movements .66. Practice alone gave .53, .42, .52, .75, .75, .73. Practice added .09 (mirror) and .08 (different) over skill.
limits: About two dozen pianists in the models. Group and practice are confounded. Simple tapping speed added no variance once practice was in the model.
agent_relevance: Supports practice as a mediator of group differences, with small N and unblinded retrospective estimates.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Strategy matters, not only repetition. A digit-span subject who only rehearsed barely improved. Subjects who used prior knowledge to encode improved greatly. One subject using retrieval structures gained over 1000%.
numbers: One subject improved by over 1000% (Chase and Ericsson 1981 data, cited). Repetition alone does not ensure top performance.
quote: providing a motivated individual with repeated exposure to a task does not ensure that the highest levels of performance will be attained
limits: Cited from earlier work, not tested in the 1993 studies themselves.
agent_relevance: Closest analogue to a scaffold: a better method for the same task, not more reps. Useful for the claim that method design drives gains.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Theory of talent: the paper rejects a major role for innate ability except for height and body size in some sports. Argues apparent talent is a predisposition and early encouragement to start deliberate practice. Elite starters begin early.
numbers: Starting age: Study 1 violinists began at 7.9 y, lessons at 8.0 y, career decision at 14.9 y. Violinists started later than pianists, F(1,40)=9.60, p<.01. Great 20th-century soloists started almost 3 y earlier than Study 1 violinists, F(1,41)=18.88, p<.001.
limits: This strong anti-talent claim was the target of later challenges (working memory, heritability, twin studies).
agent_relevance: Background: the debate is about the ceiling of practice, which an agent does not face.

source: Ericsson, Krampe, Tesch-Romer (1993) The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Origin of the 10,000 hours figure. The text says top performers reach 10,000 h of deliberate practice extended over more than a decade. It is not a threshold and the paper never says hours alone suffice.
numbers: Study 1 best violinists: 7,410 h by age 18. About 4 h per day seen as a sustainable ceiling.
limits: Popularised by Gladwell (2008); Ericsson and Harwell (2019) say he never used the term deliberate practice.
agent_relevance: Citation hygiene: do not quote 10,000 hours as an effect size.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: First formal meta-analysis of deliberate practice and performance. Mean correlation .35. Deliberate practice explained 12% of variance, leaving 88% to other factors.
numbers: 9,331 records screened, 88 studies, 111 independent samples, 157 effect sizes, total N=11,135. r=.35, 95% CI [.30,.39]. 12% variance, CI [9%,15%]. 10 of 157 correlations negative.
limits: Not corrected for unreliability: if both reliabilities are .80, r rises to .43. Inclusion needed a citation to an Ericsson paper. Ericsson and Harwell (2019) contest which effects count.
agent_relevance: The row's meta-analytic r = 0.40 matches no single reported figure: .35 (uncorrected), .43 (reliability .80), .54 and .61 in later reanalyses.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Effect varies sharply by domain. Strong for games, moderate for music and sports, weak in education, nil in professions.
numbers: Games r=.51 (26%), music r=.46 (21%), sports r=.42 (18%), education r=.21 (4%), professions r=.05, p=.62 (<1%). Domain Q(4)=49.09, p<.001.
limits: Domain is confounded with how performance and practice are measured. Professions had few effects (7 without team sports).
agent_relevance: Practice matters most in stable, rule-bound domains (games, music), the same logic as tasks with clear verifiable rewards.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Predictability of the task environment moderates the link: more predictable activity, larger effect.
numbers: High predictability r=.49 (24%), moderate r=.35 (12%), low r=.21 (4%). Q(1)=20.49, p<.001.
limits: Predictability was coded by the authors.
agent_relevance: Feedback helps only where the task has stable structure. Relevant when choosing tasks for any improvement loop.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Method of measuring practice matters: the cleaner the measure, the smaller the effect. Retrospective interview r=.45, questionnaire .34, concurrent logs .22.
numbers: Interview 20% variance, questionnaire 12%, log 5%. Q(2)=16.19, p<.001. Performance measure: group membership r=.51 (26%), lab task .37 (14%), expert rating .30 (9%), standardized objective score .28 (8%).
limits: Logs may be less complete as well as less biased. Ericsson and Harwell argue the log studies mix practice types.
agent_relevance: Hints that part of the effect is recall bias: people infer past practice from current skill.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: No sign of publication bias in the meta-analysis. Funnel plot roughly symmetric and trim-and-fill added no studies. Solitary-only practice gave a similar effect.
numbers: Excluding team sports: 119 effect sizes, 11% variance. Solitary practice only: 59 effect sizes.
limits: Bias test covered the published corpus plus requested unpublished data.
agent_relevance: Low file-drawer risk for the headline estimate; the dispute is about definition, not bias.

source: Platz, Kopiez, Lehmann, Wolf (2014) The influence of deliberate practice on musical achievement: a meta-analysis
finding: Music-only meta-analysis with strict criteria gave a much higher corrected correlation than Macnamara et al. Authors argue a correlation should not be squared into variance explained.
numbers: 13 studies from 102 candidates, N=788. Mean observed r=.54, corrected rc=.61, 95% CI [.54,.67]. Reanalysis of the studies in Hambrick et al.: I2=60.3%, Q(7)=17.7, p<.02.
quote: average aggregated corrected effect size of rc = 0.61
limits: Only 13 studies, some grey literature. Correction for attenuation needs reliabilities few studies report.
agent_relevance: The headline effect depends on inclusion rules and on correcting for noise. Both choices move r by about .25.

source: Hambrick, Altmann, Oswald, Meinz, Gobet (2014) Facing facts about deliberate practice (reply to Platz et al.)
finding: Reply to Platz: their own meta-analysis of music and chess found deliberate practice explained about one-third of reliable variance in each domain. They argue r=.61 can equally be an upper bound, because recall of practice can be inflated by skill. Other factors named: starting age, working memory, genes.
numbers: Music about 30% of variance (Hambrick et al. 2014). Platz r=.61 squared is 37%.
limits: Opinion piece. The primary Hambrick et al. paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: The same r values support opposite readings; the dispute is r versus r squared and upper versus lower bound.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: Sports meta-analysis: deliberate practice explained 18% of variance. The link vanished among elite athletes.
numbers: 52 samples, 63 effect sizes. r=.43, 95% CI [.35,.50], 18% variance, I2=83.5. Elite samples r=.11, p=.50 (1%). Sub-elite r=.44 (19%). Mixed samples r=.54 (29%). Skill level Q(2)=7.04, p=.03.
limits: High heterogeneity. Range restriction among elites could shrink r. Elite group is small.
agent_relevance: Within a skill-restricted group, extra hours did not separate better from worse, as in the later violin replication.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: Sports moderators: team vs individual, ball vs non-ball, open vs closed skill, age, and method of measuring practice did not matter. Performance measure did. Unpublished studies gave smaller effects than published ones.
numbers: Team 17% vs individual 19%. Interview 19% vs questionnaire 18%. Group-membership performance r=.50 (25%). Published r=.48 (23%, 38 cases, N=2,066) vs unpublished r=.33 (11%, 25 cases, N=699), Q(1)=4.23, p=.04. Solitary practice only: r=.47, 22%, 14 effects, N=488.
limits: Unpublished studies are mostly theses and may be lower quality. Higher-skill athletes began later, difference n.s., p=.68.
agent_relevance: A mild publication-bias signal in sports, unlike the 2014 meta-analysis.

source: Ericsson, Harwell (2019) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice on the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Reply to the meta-analyses. Says Macnamara et al. counted many activities that are not deliberate practice (school study, team play, pooled activity time). Re-coding with three criteria (reproducibly superior performance, practice aimed at the target, solitary or coached) raised the correlation.
numbers: Selected effects: r=.54, 95% CI [.44,.63], about 29% of variance vs 14% in Macnamara et al. Objective r=.49, relative r=.65. Coached r=.56, solitary r=.51, difference n.s. After correcting for attenuation they argue about 61% of variance.
quote: there was no evidence for a magical number
limits: Authors are the original theorists and chose the effects. Corrections use their own assumed reliabilities (about .6 for long-range recall).
agent_relevance: Even on the most generous reading r is about .5-.6, and 10,000 h was never in the paper. Ericsson puts international piano winners nearer 25,000 h.

source: Ericsson, Harwell (2019) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice on the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Reliability of recalled practice is limited. Diary and recall agree for the current year but poorly for decades back. Studies with fuller practice histories explain over half the variance in chess and Scrabble.
numbers: Chess diaries vs weekly estimate r(34)=.60 (de Bruin 2008). Athlete vs parent estimates r=.59 (Baker 2003). Reliability .6-.8 for the last year or two. Chess practice history over 50% of variance (Burgoyne 2019), also Scrabble (Moxley 2019).
limits: The 50% figures are cited, not checked here.
agent_relevance: Measurement error in self-reported hours is a first-order issue for any claim in this subfield.

source: Macnamara, Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Romer (1993)
finding: Direct replication of the violin study with double-blind procedure and better statistics (Cleveland Institute of Music). The core finding did not replicate: best violinists had not practiced more alone than good violinists.
numbers: Best (n=13 of 24 nominated) M=8,224 h by age 18, 95% CI [6400,10048]. Good (n about 13, inferred from df) M=9,844 [6937,12751], t(24)=-0.93, p=.364, d=-0.38. Less accomplished (n=25 in the comparison) M=4,558; good vs less d=1.33, p=.005. Group effect eta2=.26 (original .48).
quote: We did not replicate the core finding that accumulated amounts of deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level
limits: Different country, school and cohort. Small groups. Replication had 82% power for eta2=.23.
agent_relevance: The 10,000 h point holds (by age 20 both top groups passed 10,000 h alone) but it does not separate best from good.

source: Macnamara, Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Romer (1993)
finding: Teacher-designed practice (the theoretical definition) was rated less relevant than practice alone and explained no more variance than practice alone.
numbers: Teacher-designed practice to age 18: best M=6,251 h, good M=6,821 h, t(24)=-0.37, p=.717; group effect eta2=.23, p=.005. Same pattern as practice alone.
limits: Ericsson and Harwell (2019) object to changes in the interview and to the prestige gap between schools.
agent_relevance: The definition problem (who designs the practice) is unresolved in the original theory.

source: Twin study (2024) Testing the Deliberate Practice Theory: does practice reduce the heritability of musical expertise?
finding: A prediction of the theory is that genetic influence on performance should fall as practice rises. A twin study found the opposite: genetic variance stayed constant and heritability rose with more practice hours.
numbers: 6,471 twins, 1,302 complete pairs. Musical auditory discrimination: about 50% genetic, 25% shared environment, 25% residual. More practice cut shared-environment and residual variance, not the genetic part.
limits: Expertise measured with one auditory discrimination test, not performance. Lifetime hours self-reported. Author names not read from the page.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the practice-bypasses-genes claim of the 1993 paper does not hold on this measure.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Bridging VLMs and embodied intelligence with Deliberate Practice Policy Optimization (DPPO, Pelican-VL 1.0)
finding: Borrows deliberate practice as a training loop: RL finds the model's failures, hardest cases go to a teacher model for reference answers, SFT trains on them, repeat. Reports 20.3% gain over Qwen2.5-VL-72B and 10.6% over 100B-class open models.
numbers: Three RL-then-SFT loops plus a final RL phase. Saturation threshold 0.7. 7B and 72B models. 72B gain 20.3% vs base. VSI-Bench gain 54.3 for 7B. Forgetting on MMStar: 1.9 (DPPO), 5.0 (SFT), 24.8 (RL). DPPO +15.8% over RL. Items with 0 of 8 correct on VSI-Bench-MCQ fell from 800 to 500.
limits: Company preprint. Name is an analogy. No non-deliberate hard-example baseline was read. Teacher is a stronger model (InternVL 3.5).
agent_relevance: The only LLM method here that operationalises goal, feedback, repetition and rising difficulty as a loop. Training-time, so not a scaffold element for our agent.

source: Hicke et al. (2026) MedSimAI: simulation and formative feedback generation to enhance deliberate practice in medical education
finding: LLM simulated patients plus rubric feedback to support deliberate practice for medical students. Usage was modest and self-selected, and volunteers did not score higher on the exam.
numbers: 1,024 completed encounters, 410 learners, 3 US schools. Mean 2.50 cases per student; 12 students (2.9%) did 8+ cases. 88 of 179 volunteers vs 91 others at one school: no significant gain on target domains (all p>0.30). LLM scoring vs humans: 32.5% exact, 64.1% within one point, 87.0% thresholded accuracy.
limits: Self-selected, no randomisation, few cases per student. A pilot, not a test of the theory.
agent_relevance: LLM feedback is good enough for triage but not exact scoring. Practice dose was too low to test deliberate practice.

source: Fazlollahi et al. (2022) Effect of AI tutoring vs expert instruction on learning simulated surgical skills among medical students
finding: Randomised trial: an AI tutor giving metric-based feedback beat remote expert instruction and no feedback in learning a simulated brain-tumour resection. A controlled test of the feedback condition. The tutor is a rule-based system, not an LLM.
numbers: N=70 medical students (23 AI tutor, 24 instructor, 23 control), 5 five-minute feedback sessions in a 75-min session. Practice Expertise Score gain 0.66 (95% CI 0.55-0.77) vs instructor and 0.65 vs control, p<.001. Realistic resection 0.53 vs instructor, 0.49 vs control, p<.001. Blinded OSATS global scores not significant (4.63, 4.40, 3.86).
limits: Single session, volunteers, novices, remote instruction due to COVID. Tutor optimises the same metric used to score.
agent_relevance: Immediate quantified feedback tied to goals beat unstructured human feedback on a measurable task.

source: Hambrick et al. (2014) Deliberate practice: Is that all it takes to become an expert? (Intelligence 45)
finding: Meta-analysis of chess and music tested whether practice largely explains individual differences. Practice explained about one-third of reliable variance in each domain.
numbers: As described in the reply article: about 30% of variance in music; one-third per domain. Not opened.
limits: Paywalled (403). Numbers come from a reply article, not the source.
agent_relevance: See the Facing facts line.
